name: Weizenbock
title: Weizenbock: Style Guide | Craft Beer School
desc: Weizenbock explained: a strong Bavarian wheat beer with banana, clove and dark fruit. How it tastes, how to serve it, Indian pairings and examples.
tagline: A hefeweizen with the strength and richness of a bock. Banana bread in a glass.
tastes:
Weizenbock is what happens when Bavarian wheat beer meets bock strength. Schneider in Munich set the template in the early 1900s with a dark, strong wheat beer, and pale versions followed later. The recipe is a hefeweizen scaled up: at least half wheat malt, the same top-fermenting weissbier yeast, and enough extra malt to reach 7 to 9 percent.

That yeast is the star. It gives banana and clove, and at this strength those notes deepen into banana bread, baked apple, plum and raisin. Dark versions add caramel and a light chocolate edge, while pale ones stay closer to honey and fresh bread. Hops barely register. The wheat gives a soft, fluffy texture and a big head, and the high carbonation keeps a rich beer from feeling heavy. Fermentation temperature decides the balance: warmer pushes banana, cooler pushes clove, and brewers tune it to taste.

profile.look: Pale gold to dark mahogany, cloudy from yeast and wheat, with a thick, mousse-like head that lasts.
profile.aroma_flavour: Banana, clove and dark fruit such as plum and raisin over bready wheat malt. Caramel in darker versions, very little hop.
profile.mouthfeel: Medium-full, soft and creamy body from wheat, lively carbonation and a gentle warming finish.
profile.ingredients: Wheat malt as half or more of the grist, with Pilsner, Munich and some caramel malt, a little noble hop, and a weissbier yeast.

in_india: Indian drinkers already know hefeweizen, so weizenbock is an easy step up. A few Bengaluru brewpubs have poured one, and it is a good beer to try fresh from the tank because the yeast character fades with age and heat. It is strong, so share a glass or take a smaller pour. It works best on a cool evening or after a long monsoon walk rather than in May sunshine.

pairings.why: The soft, spiced meat and the beer's banana and clove share a gentle sweetness and warmth.
Tamarind tang and ghee meet a creamy wheat body that rounds off the spice.
Black pepper picks up the clove note, and the beer's malt calms the heat.
Banana meets banana, and the beer's bubbles keep the ghee in check.
